slides: The parallelogram. It's like a rectangle that someone squashed a little sideways.

slides.say: Take a rectangle and squash it a little sideways. That's a parallelogram.
Its opposite sides are equal and parallel. A D is equal and parallel to B C, and A B is equal and parallel to D C.
What do we know about the angles? Opposite angles are equal. Angle A equals angle C, and angle B equals angle D.
And any two angles next to each other add up to a hundred eighty. D and C, a hundred eighty. A and D, a hundred eighty. B and C, and A and B, also a hundred eighty.
For example, if angle B is seventy, then angle D is seventy too, and angles A and C are each a hundred ten. And if an angle is a hundred twenty-five, the angle next to it is fifty-five.
Let's see why. The opposite sides are parallel, so let's extend them into long parallel lines. These two sides are parallel too, so we extend them as well.

slides: Remember, two parallel lines and a line that cuts them make small angles and large angles. And it's the same crossing at every corner of the parallelogram.

slides.say: So all the large angles are equal, we'll call them beta, and all the small ones are equal, we'll call them alpha. That's the first rule: opposite angles are equal.
And a small angle plus a large angle is a hundred eighty. So two angles next to each other add up to a hundred eighty: alpha plus beta is a hundred eighty.
Now the diagonals. Are they equal? Not necessarily. Here there's a longer diagonal and a shorter one.
What we do know is that they cut each other in half. This part equals this part, and this part equals this one.
at: they cut each other in half

slides.say: Do they cut the parallelogram's angles in half? Not necessarily, even though sometimes it looks like it. And they're not necessarily perpendicular either.
If you're not sure, exaggerate. Draw a very wide, very low parallelogram, and draw a diagonal. You'll see right away that it doesn't cut the angle in half.

Two more facts: if the diagonals are equal, it's a rectangle, and if they're perpendicular, it's a rhombus. A general parallelogram promises only one thing about its diagonals: they cut each other in half.
The area of every parallelogram is simply base times height, a times h. The height is perpendicular to the base.
It's not the sloping side. The sloping side is longer than the height.
Be careful where you drop it. From A, the foot of the height lands on B C. From D, it would land outside B C, so first we extend B C.
Why base times height? Say we don't know the area of a parallelogram, but we do know the area of a rectangle. Let's draw a rectangle on the same base, with the same height.
The difference between them is a triangle. This triangle on the left is in the rectangle, but not in the parallelogram.
If we cut it out of the rectangle and move it to the right side, it fills exactly the part of the parallelogram that was missing. So the parallelogram has the same area as the rectangle.
The rectangle's area is base times height, so the parallelogram's area is a times h too.
Exam questions love a parallelogram with a special angle: thirty, forty-five or sixty degrees. For example, sides of eight and six, with an angle of thirty degrees at B. What is the area?
Drop the height from A. A right triangle forms, with a thirty-degree angle: a gold triangle.

The height is across from the thirty, so it's the short leg, half of the hypotenuse. The hypotenuse is the side of six, so the height is three. And the area is eight times three, which is twenty-four.
A lot of students multiply eight times six, but the sloping side is not the height.

With forty-five degrees, it's a silver triangle, and the height is the side over root two. With sixty, it's again a gold triangle, and the height is half the side times root three. And with an obtuse angle, like a hundred fifty, look at the angle next to it, which is thirty. [pause] Okay. I'll see you in the next video.
